title: Negative numbers: counting below zero
objectives: I can explain what a negative integer is and give real-life examples.
I can place positive and negative integers on a number line and compare and order them.
I can find the opposite of an integer and its distance from zero.
I can add and subtract positive numbers from negative integers using a number line.
why_it_matters: Negative numbers describe things we meet all the time: temperatures below freezing, a bank account that owes money, a diver below sea level, or a basement level in a car park. They are also the doorway to algebra, graphs and coordinates, where you will use them constantly. If you are comfortable with negative numbers now, a lot of Year 8 and Year 9 maths becomes much easier.
prior_knowledge: Adding and subtracting whole numbers confidently.
Reading a number line and a thermometer scale.
Knowing that zero is the starting point on a number line.
introduction: Imagine you check the weather before a school camp. Thredbo has an overnight forecast of −4°C and Sydney is expecting 14°C. How much colder is Thredbo? To answer that you first need a way to talk about temperatures below zero, and that is exactly what negative numbers are for. In this lesson you will learn what they mean, where they sit among the numbers you already know, how to compare them, and how to add and subtract with them. Everything you need is on this page. Work through it in order, try each example yourself before reading the solution, and have a pencil and paper ready.

sections.heading: What is a negative number?
sections.body: The whole numbers you have used since primary school (0, 1, 2, 3 and so on) are only half the story. Integers are all the whole numbers, including the ones that go below zero: ..., −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ... A negative integer is a whole number less than zero, and it is written with a minus sign in front, such as −4, which we read as 'negative four'. A positive integer is greater than zero, such as 4. Zero itself is neither positive nor negative. Negative numbers describe 'below' or 'owing' or 'less than nothing' in real situations. A temperature of −4°C means four degrees below freezing. A bank balance of −$30 means you owe $30. A height of −20 m means 20 metres below sea level, and Level −1 in a car park means the first level underground. The key idea is that the minus sign tells you which direction from zero the number lies, and the digit tells you how far. Two new words to remember: 'integer' (a whole number, positive, negative or zero) and 'opposite' (numbers the same distance from zero on opposite sides, which you will meet shortly).

sections.heading: The number line
sections.body: A number line is the best picture for integers. Draw a straight horizontal line and mark zero near the middle. Positive integers go to the right of zero in equal steps: 1, 2, 3 and so on. Negative integers go to the left of zero in equal steps: −1, −2, −3 and so on. The spacing must be equal, so −3 is exactly as far to the left of zero as 3 is to the right. As you move to the right, numbers get greater. As you move to the left, numbers get smaller. That is the single most important rule in this lesson, so say it to yourself: right is greater, left is smaller. For example, −3 is three steps left of zero. If you are at −3 and move four steps right you land on 1, because −2, −1, 0, 1 are four steps. You will use the symbols > (greater than) and < (less than): since 1 is to the right of −3, we write 1 > −3, and since −3 is to the left of 1, we write −3 < 1.

sections.heading: Comparing and ordering integers
sections.body: Comparing negative numbers can feel backwards at first, because bigger-looking digits mean smaller numbers once there is a minus sign. Use the number line to decide. Compare −9 and −2. Find them on the line: −9 is nine steps left of zero and −2 is only two steps left of zero. −9 is further left, so −9 < −2, even though 9 is greater than 2. Think about temperature: −9°C is much colder than −2°C, so it is the smaller temperature. Here are the rules that always work. Any positive number is greater than zero and zero is greater than any negative number, so every positive number is greater than every negative number. Between two negative numbers, the one closer to zero is greater. Between two positive numbers, the one further from zero is greater, as you already know. To put integers in order from least to greatest, list them from the leftmost on the number line to the rightmost. For example, to order 2, −6, 0 and −1: the negatives come first, and −6 is further left than −1, so the order is −6, −1, 0, 2.

sections.heading: Opposites and distance from zero
sections.body: Two integers are opposites when they are the same distance from zero but on opposite sides. The opposite of 5 is −5, and the opposite of −8 is 8. The opposite of 0 is 0, because it is already at zero. You can find an opposite by changing the sign. The distance of a number from zero is called its absolute value. We write it with two vertical lines: |−7| = 7, which reads 'the absolute value of negative seven is seven'. This is because −7 is 7 steps from zero. A distance is never negative, so absolute values are never negative either: |7| = 7 and |−7| = 7. Opposites always have the same absolute value. A common shortcut is 'just ignore the minus sign', and it happens to work for a single number, but remember the real meaning is distance from zero. That meaning will help you later when you work with the distance between two numbers.

sections.heading: Adding and subtracting on the number line
sections.body: Now let's calculate. A number line turns adding and subtracting into movement. Start at the first number. To add a positive number, move to the right. To subtract a positive number, move to the left. Take −3 + 5: start at −3 and move 5 steps right. The steps land on −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, so the answer is 2. Notice that three of the five steps were used to reach zero and the remaining two went past zero. Now take −2 − 4: start at −2 and move 4 steps left, landing on −3, −4, −5, −6, so −2 − 4 = −6. Subtracting made the number smaller, as it should. Finally take 4 − 7: start at 4 and move 7 steps left. Four steps take you to zero, and three more take you below zero to −3. So 4 − 7 = −3. A useful strategy is to 'cross zero in two moves': count the steps to zero first, then the steps that are left over. Always check that your answer is on the side of zero you expect: if you move left from a positive number and travel further than the number's size, you must end up negative.

worked_examples.title: Ordering temperatures
worked_examples.problem: Five towns have these overnight temperatures: −4°C, 3°C, −9°C, 0°C and −1°C. Put them in order from coldest to warmest.
steps: Coldest means least, so we are ordering from least to greatest.
Sort the numbers into negatives, zero and positives: negatives are −4, −9 and −1; zero is 0; the positive is 3.
Order the negatives using the number line. The further left, the smaller. −9 is furthest left, then −4, then −1.
Place zero after the negatives and the positive number last.
The order from coldest to warmest is −9, −4, −1, 0, 3.

worked_examples.title: Adding across zero
steps: Draw a number line and mark −3.
We are adding a positive number, so we move right. We need to move 5 steps.
From −3, three steps reach zero (−2, −1, 0).
We have 5 − 3 = 2 steps left, so move 2 more steps right past zero to land on 2.

worked_examples.title: Subtracting to go below zero
steps: For 4 − 7, start at 4. Subtracting a positive number means move left, 7 steps.
Four steps reach zero. There are 7 − 4 = 3 steps left, so move 3 more steps left to −3.
For −2 − 4, start at −2 and move 4 steps left.
The steps land on −3, −4, −5, −6, so −2 − 4 = −6.

worked_examples.title: A real situation: a bank balance
worked_examples.problem: Maya's account balance is $15. She buys a game for $25. What is her balance? Then she earns $40 mowing lawns. What is her balance now?
steps: Start with the balance: 15.
Buying the game takes away 25, so calculate 15 − 25. Start at 15 and move 25 left.
Fifteen steps reach zero and 10 more go below zero, so the balance is −$10. Maya owes $10.
Earning $40 adds 40, so calculate −10 + 40. Start at −10 and move 40 right.
Ten steps reach zero and 30 more go past it, so the balance is $30.
worked_examples.answer: After the game her balance is −$10 (she owes $10); after mowing it is $30.

guided_practice.prompt: Write each situation as an integer: (a) 12 metres below sea level, (b) a temperature of 6 degrees above zero, (c) a debt of $50.
guided_practice.hint: Below zero and debts are negative. 'Above' is positive.

guided_practice.prompt: Which is greater, −8 or −5? Use a number line or temperatures to explain.
guided_practice.hint: Which is closer to zero? Think about which temperature is warmer.
guided_practice.answer: −5 is greater because it is further right on the number line (closer to zero). −8°C is colder.

guided_practice.hint: Negatives first, zero, then positives. Which negative is furthest left?

guided_practice.prompt: What is the opposite of −12? What is |−12|?
guided_practice.hint: Opposites are the same distance from zero on the other side.
How many steps to reach zero from −6? How many steps are left?
guided_practice.answer: 3 (6 steps to reach zero, then 3 more to the right).

guided_practice.prompt: Work out −4 − 5. Then solve this: a diver is at −15 m and swims up 6 m. Where is she now?
guided_practice.hint: Subtract means move left. Swimming up is moving towards zero, so add.

activities.title: Temperature detective
activities.instructions: Imagine these overnight low temperatures were recorded on one winter night: Charlotte Pass −8°C, Thredbo −5°C, Canberra −2°C, Hobart 3°C, Sydney 9°C. Use the table to answer the tasks below on paper. Draw a number line from −10 to 10 first if it helps.

tasks.prompt: Write the five places in order from coldest to warmest.
tasks.answer: Charlotte Pass (−8), Thredbo (−5), Canberra (−2), Hobart (3), Sydney (9).

tasks.prompt: By the next morning Canberra warmed by 6 degrees. What was its temperature? (Calculate −2 + 6.)
Hobart then cooled by 5 degrees from 3°C. What was its temperature? (Calculate 3 − 5.)
How many degrees warmer is Sydney than Charlotte Pass? Count the steps on your number line.
tasks.answer: 17 degrees (8 steps to zero and 9 more).

activities.title: Draw and jump on a number line
activities.instructions: Use a ruler to draw a number line on paper from −10 to 10, with equal spaces and every integer labelled. Complete each task using your line.

tasks.answer: Each point sits at the correct step from zero; negatives are left of zero.

tasks.prompt: List two pairs of opposites from the numbers you marked and from their opposites.
tasks.answer: For example 4 and −4, −7 and 7, 9 and −9, −2 and 2.

tasks.prompt: Start at −8 and jump 11 steps right. Where do you land?
Start at 2 and jump 9 steps left. Where do you land?

activities.title: Money story
activities.instructions: Maya starts with a balance of $0. Calculate her balance after each event, drawing a number line for each step if you need to.

tasks.prompt: Her allowance of $10 arrives. Was she ever in debt, and when?
tasks.answer: Her balance is $7. Yes: after the game (−$25) and after lunch (−$3).

questions.prompt: Explain in your own words what −5 means in three different real-life situations (for example temperature, money and height).
questions.answer_key: Any three accurate situations, e.g. 5 degrees below zero, a debt or balance of −$5, 5 metres below sea level or 5 levels underground.

questions.prompt: Put these in order from least to greatest: −3, 5, −11, 0, −8.
Explain why −9 is less than −2 even though 9 is greater than 2.
questions.answer_key: On the number line −9 is further left than −2, so it is smaller. Or: −9°C is colder than −2°C; a debt of $9 is worse than a debt of $2.

questions.prompt: Work out −7 + 10 and 5 − 12. Show the steps on a number line.
questions.answer_key: −7 + 10 = 3 (7 steps to zero, 3 more). 5 − 12 = −7 (5 steps to zero, 7 more left).

questions.prompt: Sam says −4 + 3 = −7. What mistake did Sam make and what is the correct answer?
questions.answer_key: Sam moved the wrong way (or added the number parts and kept the minus). Adding 3 moves right: −4 + 3 = −1.

questions.prompt: A lift starts at level −2 (the second basement) and goes up 5 levels. Which level does it reach? Show the calculation.

quiz.question: Which of these is the lowest temperature?
quiz.explanation: −10 is furthest left on the number line, so it is the least.

quiz.question: Which statement is true?
quiz.explanation: −6 is to the left of −2, so −6 < −2.

quiz.question: What is the opposite of 14?
quiz.explanation: Opposites are the same distance from zero on the other side.

quiz.question: What is −5 + 8?
quiz.explanation: Five steps reach zero, then three more steps to the right: 3.

quiz.question: What is 3 − 9?
quiz.explanation: Three steps reach zero, then six more steps left: −6.

quiz.question: What is |−11|?
quiz.explanation: The absolute value is the distance from zero, which is 11.

misconceptions.mistake: '−9 is greater than −2 because 9 is greater than 2.'
misconceptions.fix: With negative numbers the order flips. Find both on a number line: −9 is further left, so it is smaller. Check with temperatures: −9°C is colder than −2°C.

misconceptions.mistake: '−4 + 3 = −7': adding the digits and keeping the minus sign.
misconceptions.fix: Adding a positive number always moves right on the number line. From −4, move 3 steps right to −1. The answer must be greater than −4.

misconceptions.mistake: 'Zero is a negative number' or 'zero is positive'.
misconceptions.fix: Zero is the dividing point. It is neither positive nor negative.

misconceptions.mistake: 'The absolute value of −7 is −7' or 'absolute value means take away the number'.
misconceptions.fix: Absolute value is a distance from zero, and a distance is never negative. |−7| = 7.

consolidation: Let's pull together what you have learned. Integers are the whole numbers, including negatives, zero and positives. On a number line, right is greater and left is smaller, so −9 < −2 and every negative is less than every positive. Opposites are the same distance from zero on opposite sides, and the absolute value of a number is its distance from zero. To add a positive number you move right; to subtract a positive number you move left; and when you pass zero, count the steps to zero first and then the steps left over. If you can explain these ideas to someone else using a number line or a thermometer, you have understood them.
support: If you find this hard: (1) use a real thermometer or draw a vertical number line like one, and talk about 'warmer' and 'colder'; (2) always draw the number line and put a pencil dot on the starting number before moving; (3) practise with small numbers first, such as −2 + 3 and 1 − 3, before using larger ones; (4) use a money story: negative means you owe; (5) say each calculation in words, such as 'negative three plus five'.
extension: Challenge yourself: (1) How many integers are there between −6 and 4, not counting −6 and 4? (2) A sequence starts at 12 and goes down by 5 each time. Write the first six terms and say which term is the first negative. (3) Invent a word problem about temperature whose answer is −7, and swap it with someone to solve.
materials: A thermometer or today's weather forecast (optional)
parent_script: This is an independent lesson, so you do not need to teach it. Suggested check-ins: (1) After the 'Comparing and ordering' section (about 20 minutes in), ask your child to explain, without looking, why −9 is less than −2. (2) When they reach the worked examples, check they are drawing number lines and not only reading. (3) After the activities, mark the written questions using the answer key; look for the number line reasoning, not just the answer. (4) If they score fewer than 4 out of 6 on the quiz, have them redo the number line activity tomorrow and re-read the section on adding and subtracting. Suggested timing: sections about 20 minutes, worked examples about 10, guided practice about 10, activities about 12, questions and quiz about 8.

teaching_questions.ask: Which is greater, −9 or −2, and how do you know?
teaching_questions.expected: −2, because it is further right on the number line and closer to zero.

teaching_questions.ask: What does a bank balance of −$20 mean?
teaching_questions.expected: The account owes $20, or is $20 overdrawn.

teaching_questions.ask: Why must the answer to −4 + 3 be greater than −4?
teaching_questions.expected: Adding a positive number moves right, so the answer is greater.

evidence_suggestions: A photo of the child's hand-drawn number line with the jumps marked.
The written explanation of why −9 is less than −2.
The completed temperature detective and money story working.
A note of the quiz result and whether the child could explain a mistake in their own words.

offline_alternative: All the learning can be done on paper with a ruler. The only on-screen parts are the quiz and handing in.
parent_notes: Reference example (not AI output) showing the depth a Side-Quest lesson should reach for an independent secondary lesson.
teaching_plan: Concept: negative integers, their order, opposites and adding or subtracting a positive number using a number line. Prior knowledge: whole-number arithmetic and reading number lines or thermometers. Progression: (1) what negative numbers mean in real situations; (2) place them on a number line; (3) compare and order them, correcting the belief that a bigger digit means a bigger number; (4) opposites and absolute value as distance from zero; (5) add and subtract a positive number by moving right or left, crossing zero in two moves; (6) apply it to temperature and money. Likely misconceptions: −9 > −2, adding digits and keeping the sign, zero being negative, absolute value being negative. Assessment: ordering, explanation, calculation across zero, spot-the-mistake, real-world problem and a short quiz.
